source: Morais O., Cargill C., Parke K. and Barnes T. 2020. Smallholder Pig Production Technicians' Manual. Timor-Leste Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, University of Queensland, ACIAR and the TOMAK Program (Australian Aid), Dili.
text: There are three main ways to raise pigs. Free-roaming/scavenging is cheapest and needs little labour, but pigs waste energy searching for food, mix with other farmers' pigs (spreading disease), can eat dog/cat/human faeces (risking cysticercosis and toxoplasmosis, which make the meat unsafe), may eat toxic plants, and piglets born outside the house are often killed by the sow or predators before the farmer finds them. Semi-intensive systems confine pigs in a pen overnight with a small outside paddock for foraging during the day; intensive systems confine pigs fully in pens. Both semi-intensive and intensive systems cost more in labour and infrastructure but keep pigs isolated from other animals' faeces and diseases, protect against predators, and result in healthier, faster-growing pigs with greater profit per pig.
caveat: This guidance comes from a Timor-Leste smallholder pig manual, not a Cambodia-specific source. Feed ingredients and general husbandry practices transfer well to Cambodia's tropical smallholder conditions, but local breed weights/ages and disease-context details may differ; confirm specifics with a local vet or extension officer where precision matters.
